You are comparing two drafts written from the same brief. Read no other file, and do not run commands or browse; judge only the text below.

Brief: Write the docs-site page for the `term-weave` skill with the sections What it does, When to use it, How it works, and What you get.

<<<DRAFT A
# term-weave

## What it does

`term-weave` drafts a glossary of project terms from documents in a supplied folder. Every drafted definition links to the passage that supports it.

## When to use it

Use it when project vocabulary is scattered across documents or newcomers encounter unexplained terms.

## How it works

Run the skill manually:

```text
/term-weave <source-folder>
```

It reads Markdown and plain-text documents in the supplied folder and ignores other file types.

If the folder is missing or contains no readable supported documents, it stops and explains the problem without drafting.

The skill does not invent definitions. It lists terms without a supporting explanation under **Unresolved terms**.

If sources give conflicting definitions, it preserves both in one entry, links each source, and marks the entry **Conflict**.

## What you get

The skill writes `GLOSSARY.md` in the working directory. Entries appear alphabetically, with **Unresolved terms** after the defined entries.

The source documents remain unchanged.

<<<DRAFT B
## What it does

`term-weave` drafts a glossary of project terms from documents in a folder you supply.

## When to use it

Use it when project vocabulary is scattered across documents or newcomers encounter unexplained terms.

## How it works

Run the skill manually with a source folder:

```text
/term-weave <source-folder>
```

For example, if your documents are in `./docs`, run:

```text
/term-weave ./docs
```

The skill reads Markdown and plain-text documents and ignores other file types. If the folder is missing or contains no readable supported documents, it stops and explains the problem without drafting.

Each drafted definition links to the passage that supports it. The skill does not invent definitions. It places terms without a supporting explanation under **Unresolved terms**.

When sources give conflicting definitions, it keeps both in one entry, links each source, and marks the entry **Conflict**.

## What you get

The skill writes `GLOSSARY.md` in your working directory. Defined entries appear alphabetically, followed by **Unresolved terms**. Your source documents remain unchanged.
DRAFT B>>>

items.title: Thinking
items.text:
I'm weighing the two versions against each other. Version A opens with a title heading and puts the "links to passage" point under What it does, while B drops the H1 but has a concrete example and places that point under How it works. Both carry the same facts, and B speaks to the reader more directly with "you" and "your." The missing title in B could read as an omission, though a docs site may generate it anyway, so I'm leaning toward B, with the example and tone tipping it.

I'm now settling on B: the concrete example and the reader-directed "you" tip it, even though the missing title is a fair point to weigh. A's placement of the link fact under What it does is stronger than B's thinner version, so I'm holding that as a careful caveat rather than a deciding factor.
